If pancreatitis occurs, discontinue the drug immediately. For other adverse drug reactions (ADRs), consider reducing the dose. 2. The use of this medication in combination with other antiretroviral drugs may increase the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Additionally, there is a risk of retinal changes and optic neuritis. 3. The drug degrades rapidly in acidic pH; however, enteric coating (EC) protects it from stomach acids. 4. Non-cirrhotic portal hypertension has been reported with this medication. If signs or symptoms occur, such as elevated liver enzymes, esophageal varices, hematemesis, ascites, or splenomegaly, discontinue the drug. 5. Co-administration of methadone with Videx pediatric powder may significantly decrease didanosine concentrations. 6. Patients treated with this drug in combination with stavudine may have an increased risk of pancreatitis, lactic acidosis, and hepatic toxicity. Co-administration of these drugs is contraindicated. 7. Treatment with this medication has been associated with the loss of subcutaneous fat, most notably in the face, limbs, and buttocks. The incidence and severity of lipoatrophy are related to cumulative exposure and are often not reversible even after discontinuation of treatment. Patients should be frequently examined and questioned for signs of lipoatrophy. If feasible, therapy should be switched to an alternative regimen if lipoatrophy is suspected. 8. To monitor maternal-fetal outcomes in pregnant women exposed to didanosine and other antiretroviral agents, an Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry has been established. Physicians are encouraged to register patients by calling 1-800-258-4263. 9. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of didanosine in pregnant women. The drug should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. 10. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend that HIV-infected mothers should not breastfeed their infants to avoid the risk of postnatal transmission of HIV. A study in rats showed that following oral administration, didanosine and/or its metabolites were excreted into the milk of lactating rats. It is not known if didanosine is excreted in human milk. Due to the potential for HIV transmission and serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, mothers receiving didanosine should be instructed not to breastfeed. 11. Didanosine is generally considered acceptable during pregnancy. Controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk. 12. The half-life of didanosine in adults is approximately 5 hours. 13. Before dispensing, pharmacists must reconstitute the dry powder to an initial concentration of 20 mg/mL and immediately mix the resulting solution with an antacid to achieve a final concentration of 10 mg/mL. 14. To prepare the initial solution (20 mg/mL), reconstitute the product by adding 100 mL or 200 mL of purified water USP to the 2 g or 4 g of powder, respectively. 15. To prepare the final solution (10 mg/mL), immediately mix one part of the 20 mg/mL initial solution with one part of any commercially available antacid containing aluminum hydroxide (400 mg/5 mL), magnesium hydroxide (400 mg/5 mL), and simethicone (40 mg/5 mL). 16. The oral solution is dispensed as 10 mg/mL with an antacid as the diluent. It should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before food or 2 hours after food. The maximum concentration (Cmax) and area under the curve (AUC) are reduced by approximately 46% and 19%, respectively, in the presence of food. 17. The enteric-coated (EC) formulation is not approved for use in children under 6 years of age or in children who weigh less than 20 kg and are unable to swallow capsules whole. 18. The reconstituted oral solution (10 mg/mL) should be refrigerated at 36–46°F (2–8°C) and used within 30 days. Any unused portion should be discarded after 30 days. 19.
